<header>BOOK IV.</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: the power of understanding. Look at the explanation of this composition, and consider it for a long time; and the longer you have considered it, the more you will judge the artifice to be admirable. Delay is demanded, and that not for anything, but for touching. For we consider things so that we may attain their nature. Touch again is not of any thing; but of that which alone we ought to wish with all prayers to touch. Which the conversion of the word itself warns us, which <term>Car</term> brings forth.</meta> 
<note>continues from previous page: ...as the doctrine of words may show, and the analytical consideration of <term>Cram</term> itself may teach us, that it alone is the shop first and most worthy of this name, which demonstrates to us God himself extended on the cross; we understand that all the attention of our mind ought to be occupied in this, that we may always and everywhere think as diligently as possible about the extension of charity on the cross, which is the widest of all and embraces every happiness; and we judge this to be that consideration toward which the architect of the word looked, aiming at this in all words, that their rationale might always be discerned as most excellent in the highest things which are comprehended by the breadth of their signification. And these things indeed concerning <term>Marc</term> and <term>Cram</term>, truly wonderful and divine words, and not without the instinct of the divine spirit either fashioned by the first craftsman or resolved by me into their causes. But if we must explain how widely the extension, which is denoted by the <term>fiam</term> <gloss>becoming/extension</gloss>, reaches, a forest of things most worthy of consideration would fail us before the day ended. This, however, must not be passed over in silence, that this word <margin>tant:</margin> not only signifies to extend, but is also in frequent use for that which is to bring a matter happily to perfection without any fault or error. What is more fitting to the extension of <term>car</term> <gloss>dear/love</gloss> than this very thing? What declares more clearly the reason why that dear Son of God was extended? Was it not for this, that He might unfold, and, to follow the common use of the word, smooth out the human race to the ultimate end of supreme perfection? Although this is indeed the true and primary fabrication of <term>Marc</term> itself, it nevertheless passes to other things, in which, although it may not be that highest cause of consideration, there is still something useful and often necessary for the common way of life, lest the supreme consideration of the highest shop suffer an impediment. For since without peace, which Christ our master is accustomed to pray for every house, you can neither behold nor consider that supreme shop with any fruit, nor can peace consist without justice, which gives to each his own; it was necessary to note diligently what belongs to each, and to distinguish it with certain signs, lest any controversy should disturb the common tranquility. Therefore, they also called such a sign <term>Marc</term>, because of its necessary consideration, which <margin>marc: marca.</margin> is indeed a boundary in some regions, and in others a mark proper to each individual's property. The Italians and Spaniards borrowed the same word from the Goths, which, as long as it remains to them, will be <term>Marca</term> <gloss>March/Mark</gloss>, the Latin language having been reduced to this form by the phrases and words of the Teutons, as it is now both written and sounded, which they call Roman. Hence the March of Ancona, the March of Treviso, and very many other boundaries. Hence border-counts were called <margin>Marchionel:</margin> Marquises. Hence <term>Marca</term> among them was made for any mark for recognizing what is proper to each. Furthermore, just as our countrymen usually say <term>mer</term> for <term>mar</term> and for <term>moror</term> <gloss>I delay</gloss>, so also they almost always pronounce <margin>Mer: Merc.</margin> <term>merc</term> for <term>marc</term>: which not only our people do, but the upper Germans also do. Nor do the words retained by the first peoples, whether Cimmerians or Gauls, declare otherwise than that the ancient Gauls pronounced <term>Merx</term> and <term>Mercurius</term>. Therefore, the Latins made <term>Merx</term> <margin>Merx; mer- ca. Merc.</margin> from our word <term>meret</term> <gloss>market</gloss>, by which we note the forum, since for them a venal thing is so called. The forum is called <term>meret</term> from the imperative, as if you were to say, "Consider what you buy or sell." For there is need of no small consideration in buying and selling: he who lacks this, I do not think the forum should be frequented by him. Oblique cases declare that <term>Merx</term> is derived from <term>mere</term>; and soon from there the verb <margin>Mercor, ari.</margin> <term>Mercor</term> <gloss>I trade</gloss> with its offspring. From <term>mere</term> also comes <term>mere-ur</term> <gloss>to merit/deserve</gloss>, for one who has perfect excellence of consideration, which, since it exists only with God, this name is consecrated to God. That <term>Dè</term> <gloss>God</gloss> is said to be excellent in every kind, and its contrary to be <term>tu</term> <gloss>thou/you</gloss>, I have both said more frequently, and indicated a little while ago. But as to the fact that this is the name of God, it must not be understood in such a way that one God is here, and another is the true and supreme God. There is one God, not many; one, I say, one, yet He can be invoked by as many names as there are various vows of mortals, and with as much varied efficacy as He possesses. Thus the religion of the Druids should be understood, and unless it is so understood, it will be called not the religion of the Druids, that is, of the teachers of truth, but the superstition and idol-mania of the fabricators of impiety. Thus they thought, as other things demonstrate, so also the Alphabet itself, which the Latins retained: in which the discourse is destined from the very beginning to the One Himself. Not one Jupiter, another Mercury, another Mars, another Apollo, another Hercules, another Minerva, another Juno, another Venus, but one God is all things in all, being the internal principle of all goods, whatever they may be. Therefore, although <margin>Why many names are attributed to God:</margin> other goods are expressed by other names, all words noting the source of any of them are taken for one God: nor does the diversity of words indicate anything other than the diversity of goods flowing from one source.</note>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...in number between two extremes, just as one motion of two extremes, which is false; rather, there are two relations differing in number, sometimes in species, sometimes in genus. In number only, as when one equal is related to another. For two equals are related to each other by relations differing only in number. In species, however, as the relatives above of position and supposition are related to each other by relations differing in species, just as the relation of a master differs in species from the relation of a servant. In genus, however, when the relatives are of such a condition that one is related by a real relation and the other by a relation of reason, then they are related by relations differing in genus, such as knowledge and the knowable.</meta>

### That a relation can exist between two extremes that is not real.
### Cap. CLXXXIII.

<note>A decorative initial Q starts the chapter.</note>

Regarding the eighth, it can be concluded that it is not necessary, if the relation of one extreme is real, that the relation of the other extreme be real. And therefore it is not the same to say that a relation is real and that it has two real extremes, because it can have two real extremes and yet be a relation of reason; however, it cannot be the opposite, namely, to be a real relation without two real extremes. Nor is it the same to say that a relation is real and that it has a corresponding real relation in the opposite terminus, because it can be real without this. Whence, having a corresponding real relation in the opposite terminus adds to that which is being a real relation.
